<text><loc_47><loc_158><loc_243><loc_267>Accurate document layout analysis is a key requirement for high-quality PDF document conversion. Version with the recent availability of public, large ground-truth datasets such as PubLayNet and DocBank, deep-learning models have proven to be very effective at layout detection and segmentation. While these datasets are of adequate size to train such models, they severely lack in layout variability since they are sourced from scientific article repositories such as PubMed and arXiv only. <section_header_level_1><loc_27><loc_147><loc_75><loc_155>ABSTRACT</section_header_level_1>
<text><loc_27><loc_157><loc_225><loc_333>Accurate document layout analysis is a key requirement for high-quality PDF document conversion. With recent availability of public, large ground-truth datasets such as PubLayNet and DocBank, deep-learning models have proven to be very effective at layout detection and segmentation. While these datasets are of adequate size to train such models, they severely lack in layout variability since they are sourced from scientific article repositories such as PubMed and arXiv only. Consequently, the accuracy of the layout segmentation drops significantly when these models are applied on more challenging and diverse layouts. In this paper, we present a new, publicly available, document-layout annotation dataset in COCO format. It contains 80863 manually annotated pages from diverse data sources to represent a wide variety of layouts. For each PDF page, the layout annotations provide label-based bounding-box features of each distinct class. We also provide a subset of double- and triple-annotated pages to determine the inter-annotator agreement. In multiple experiments, we provide baseline accuracy scores for each class. We also demonstrate that these models fall approximately 10% behind the inter-annotator agreement. Furthermore, we provide evidence that DocLayNet is of sufficient size. Lastly, we compare models trained on PubLayNet, DocBank, and DocLayNet, showing that layout predictions of the DocLayNet-trained models are more robust than the preferred choice for general-purpose document-layout analysis.</text>
